Adler & Lillian Adler Collection, Cincinnati (acquired from the above on January 3, 1950). | Emma Margaret Goldman Collection, Cincinnati (by descent from the above). | Thence by descent to the present owner. | | | Marc Chagall's Les amoureux is a radiant celebration of one of the artist's most enduring themes: the triumph of love as the ultimate human experience. Executed circa 1938, this romantic composition encapsulates the painter's conviction that love was not merely a subject but the very essence of art itself. As Chagall would later reflect: 'In it lies the true Art: from it comes my technique, my religion... Art, without Love... would open the wrong door' (the artist, quoted in J. Baal-Teshuva (ed.), Chagall: A Retrospective, Westport, 1995, p. 179). Nowhere is this credo more poignantly expressed than in the tender embrace of the figures at the heart of this work, who embody both personal devotion and universal harmony. | | The composition presents a pair of lovers seated on a rustic wooden bench; their forms united in a gesture of profound intimacy. The male figure, rendered in glowing red tones, leans protectively toward his companion, who is enveloped in the serene coolness of blue. The chromatic contrast of their garments - fiery passion tempered by tranquil devotion - creates a visual metaphor for balance within unity. Their faces, softly illuminated and delicately modeled, radiate a serenity that transcends the earthly moment, suggesting that the embrace captures not a fleeting instant but an eternal state of communion. Hovering in the upper left of the composition, an angelic figure reaches forward with an olive branch, blessing the couple with both divine sanction and symbolic peace. The motif recalls biblical messengers and the longstanding artistic tradition of the olive branch as an emblem of hope and reconciliation. Here, the celestial gesture elevates the earthly embrace, transforming a private moment into a vision of universal love. Chagall, who frequently combined personal imagery with spiritual symbolism, succeeds in making his own life's passion - his devotion to his wife Bella - an emblem of love in its most transcendent form. | | The dreamlike palette, dominated by radiant blues and verdant greens, envelops the scene in an atmosphere of otherworldly calm. Although grounded by the bench and the grassy knoll, the figures seem suspended within a realm outside of time. This balance between earthly intimacy and ethereal detachment is characteristic of Chagall's oeuvre, in which lovers soar over rooftops, float among village squares, or, as in Les amoureux, inhabit a serene landscape infused with memory and longing. | | The poignancy of this work is heightened when considered in relation to the circumstances of its creation. Executed in the late 1930s, Les amoureux emerged at a moment of escalating turmoil in Europe. Having been granted French citizenship in 1937, Chagall and his wife Bella settled in the countryside, first in St. Dyé-sur-Loire and later in Gordes, Provence. Yet the world around them was rapidly destabilizing. In May 1940, Germany invaded Belgium and Holland; by June, Paris had fallen. While many contemporaries fled, Chagall hesitated, immersing himself in his work even as the threat to Jewish artists grew dire. It was only through the intervention of Varian Fry and the Emergency Rescue Committee in 1941 that the Chagalls escaped to New York, carrying with them the memory of a Europe they were uncertain to see again. | | In this context, Les amoureux assumes a dual resonance. It is, on one level, a deeply personal tribute to Bella, whose presence animated Chagall's imagination throughout his career. Yet it is also a symbolic refuge, a declaration of love's permanence in the face of dislocation and uncertainty. While war consumed Europe, Chagall's composition affirmed the resilience of human connection. The painting thus embodies both private devotion and a universal message: that love endures, unassailable, even against the backdrop of history's darkest upheavals. | | Chagall's Les amoureux stands as a testament to his singular vision, one in which the intimate and the eternal, the personal and the universal, are seamlessly intertwined. With its vivid colors, poetic symbolism, and profound emotional resonance, the work captures the essence of the artist's lifelong pursuit: to transform memory and emotion into timeless images of love, hope, and transcendence.

This period included a great deal of work, both elaborating and synthesizing. The slightest alteration was pondered for a long time and worked out with the help of fresh drawings. Because a change in one place affects the balance of the whole, one is often obliged to rework the whole construction of the picture" (F. Léger quoted in J. Cassou & J. The cup's position between their faces creates a dreamlike optical illusion, a surreal interplay where Dalí reminds us that the lovers themselves embody the very source of their downfall. | | The piece was first owned by Joseph Wandy, an employee of the Rowland Development Corporation, the company behind Rowlux, a three-dimensional plastic sheeting. In 1972, Dalí partnered with the firm to create an artwork using this innovative material, continuing his fascination with experimental mediums like holograms and dimensional plastics. provenance: The artist's studio, Long Island. | Thomas Craven Collection, Martha's Vineyard. | Private collection, Massachusetts. | Acquired from the above by the previous owner; their sale, Christie's, New York, May 14, 2021, lot 462. | Acquired at the above sale by the present owner. | | | These lovely Christmas greetings by George Grosz were dedicated from him and his wife Eve to Thomas Craven (1888-1969), the famous author, art critic and lecturer. Grosz had befriended Craven in the late 1930s, and he made several portrait studies of him. Craven was also very fond of Grosz and included him in his esteemed bestseller A Treasury of Art Masterpieces. From the Renaissance to the Present Day (New York, Simon & Schuster, 1939). Craven selected a watercolor by Grosz from the year 1928 to be reproduced in the book Ein Mann von Überzeugung/Ein Hakenkreuzritter (A Man of Opinion), which today is in the Collection of the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, D.C. | | Thomas Craven, who also promoted other American artists like Thomas Hart Benton, John Stuart Curry and Grant Wood, was, however, a vehement critic of the Paris School. Grosz did not agree with him about this crusade. With fine cynical insinuation, without being offensive, Grosz portrayed Craven in his Christmas card as a fearless dragon-slayer, dressed in medieval costume with his initials 'Th.Cr.' on his doublet. Craven fights the French Dragon, a legendary dragon-like mythological hybrid from Provence in Southern France, but in this case, without any doubt, represents the School of Paris. | | Excerpted text by Ralph Jentsch.
